title: The learning loop
purpose: See the four steps of the learning loop as one repeatable cycle.
explanation: Read, build, measure, and explain form one loop: each step feeds the next, and explaining leads back to reading the next topic. This is the method the whole roadmap follows.
alt: Four steps in a circle: read the primary doc, build a small demo, measure in DevTools, then explain or teach it, which leads back to reading.

learning_check.question: Which step starts the next loop?
learning_check.answer: Explain, because teaching a topic shows the next gap to read about.

title: How a feature gains a Baseline status
purpose: See that a Baseline status changes only because of browser support and the passage of time.
explanation: A feature starts at Limited availability while browsers disagree about it. When all four core browsers support it, it becomes Newly available on the newly interoperable date. Thirty months later it becomes Widely available, and most sites can then use it without worrying about support.
alt: State diagram with three states in a row: Limited availability, then Newly available once every core browser supports the feature, then Widely available after 30 months pass.

learning_check.question: A feature became Newly available in December 2023. In which month does it become Widely available?
learning_check.answer: June 2026, which is 30 months after December 2023.

title: Feature detection: one question, two test paths, two outcomes
purpose: See that both the CSS at-rule and the JavaScript call ask the same feature question, and that both end in an enhanced path or a fallback path.
explanation: The page needs one feature, here a subgrid layout. MDN gives two ways to ask whether the browser has it: the @supports at-rule in CSS and the CSS.supports() call in JavaScript. Both answers go to the same place. A yes applies the enhanced layout and a no applies the fallback layout, so the page always renders. The dashed arrow marks the wrong question. Reading the user agent string to name the browser replaces the feature question with a guess, and MDN discourages it.
alt: Flowchart: a need for a subgrid layout leads to the question 'is the feature supported?'. That question splits into a CSS test using @supports and a JavaScript test using CSS.supports. Both tests lead to 'enhanced layout applies' on yes and 'fallback layout applies' on no. A separate box asks the wrong question, which browser is this, and points to the feature question instead.

learning_check.question: Which of the two tests needs no JavaScript?
learning_check.answer: The @supports at-rule, because the browser runs the test itself while it parses the CSS.

title: The four modules of the zustand library
purpose: See that the React binding, the middlewares and the build machinery all depend on one small core store.
explanation: The core store holds the state and the listeners. The React binding subscribes to that store and reads a snapshot. Every middleware reaches the store by replacing one method on the store object, and the build machinery bundles and tests both layers.
alt: A module map with four boxes: the React binding points at the core store with 'subscribe and read', the middleware points at the core store with 'replace setState', and the build machinery points at both the core store and the middleware with 'bundle and test'.

learning_check.question: Which module does the React binding write to?
learning_check.answer: None. The binding subscribes and reads a snapshot, so a write always goes through the store api, which a middleware can replace.

title: One write through the zustand store
purpose: Follow one state change from a component, through the store and the persist middleware, back to the component.
explanation: A component writes a patch, the persist middleware takes it first, and the store compares the next value with the current one before it merges the patch. The listeners run with the new and the previous state, the middleware saves the part of the state it was told to keep, and the component re-renders only when its own slice changed.
alt: A sequence of four participants: the component asks the React binding for a slice, the binding subscribes and reads a snapshot, the component writes a patch that the persist middleware passes on, the store compares and merges the patch and notifies its listeners, the middleware saves the state, and the binding returns the slice to the component.

learning_check.question: Why does the component not always re-render after a write?
learning_check.answer: The React binding runs the selector again and compares the slice, so only a component whose own slice changed re-renders.

title: The Baseline ship decision
purpose: Decide whether a feature is safe to ship by tracing it through the Baseline labels.
explanation: A feature stays at Limited availability until all four core browsers, Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Safari, ship it. Once they all do, it becomes Newly available, which means the browsers agree on how it behaves, so it is safe to ship. After 30 months it becomes Widely available and can ship freely.
alt: A decision tree: a new feature is Limited and should be held off until all four core browsers ship it; then it is Newly available and safe to ship; after 30 months it becomes Widely available and can ship freely.

learning_check.question: A feature is Limited today. What must happen before you ship it?
learning_check.answer: All four core browsers must ship it, which makes it Newly available.

title: Publishing on MDN: the review loop
purpose: See that publishing on MDN is a review loop, not a one-shot upload.
explanation: A contribution to MDN starts when you pick a task from the board, claim it, and tag the MDN community team so a mentor can find it. You open a pull request, get the writing reviewed, and the page goes live. Teaching in public is this loop: write it, ship it, and let a reviewer correct what you missed.
alt: Six steps in a row: pick a task, claim it and tag the MDN community team, get hints from a mentor, open a pull request, get the writing reviewed, and the page is published.

learning_check.question: Which step catches the mistakes you did not know you made?
learning_check.answer: The review, because a reviewer checks the writing and asks you to fix what you got wrong.

title: How the ship-it checker decides
purpose: See the order in which the checker reads the Baseline snapshot, decides the verdict, and writes the runtime check.
explanation: The command line picks the target and the feature ids. The lookup finds each feature in the Baseline snapshot, the decision compares the feature's status with the target, and the detection step writes the runtime check for the fallback. The report prints one block per feature.
alt: Flowchart: the Baseline table and the command line feed the feature lookup, which feeds the ship decision, which feeds the runtime check, which feeds the report, which prints the verdict.

learning_check.question: Which step turns a Baseline status into a runtime check?
learning_check.answer: The decision step, because it knows the feature needs a fallback and asks the detection step for the check that goes with it.

title: How the learning log scaffolds and checks a note
purpose: See how one command scaffolds the four steps of the loop and how the check command finds the empty ones.
explanation: The create command builds a note with one empty section for each step of the learning loop, then writes it under a dated file name. The check command reads a note you filled in and names every step whose section still holds no text, so the four steps stay visible until each one has content.
alt: Two commands share one note file: the create command writes a note with four empty sections and a dated name, and the check command reads a filled note and names the steps that still hold no text.

learning_check.question: Which step does the check command name when you leave the Measure section empty?
learning_check.answer: measure, because the validator reports every step whose section holds no text yet.
